title: The Priests' Chambers and the Wall of Separation
summary: The guide leads Ezekiel to two large buildings of chambers, on the north and south sides of the temple courtyard, arranged in three stepped stories. These are holy chambers where the priests eat the most holy offerings and change out of the garments they wear to minister. Finally the guide measures the whole temple area from outside: a perfect square of five hundred cubits on each side, enclosed by a wall to separate the holy from the common.
story: The tour that began at the outer wall in chapter 40 and reached the Most Holy Place in chapter 41 now turns to the supporting structures and then to the boundary of the whole complex. With the measuring finished, the stage is set for the most important moment of the vision: the return of the glory of the LORD through the east gate in chapter 43. This chapter's closing words state the purpose of everything measured so far. The wall exists to separate the holy from the common, the very distinction Israel's priests had failed to keep (22:26), and whose collapse had driven God's presence from the old temple.
historical:
The vision is part of the unit dated to about 573 BC (40:1), when the exiles had been without a temple for more than a decade. In Solomon's temple, too, there were storerooms and chambers around the courts where priests and Levites kept supplies and carried out their duties (1 Chronicles 9:26-27; 28:12), though the Old Testament doesn't describe them in detail. Ezekiel's design gives these rooms a clear and regulated role.

The final square is large, roughly 260 meters (about 850 feet) on each side if the long cubit is used. The Hebrew of verses 16 to 19 reads five hundred rods, which would make each side six times longer, but most translations, following the ancient Greek version and in keeping with the parallel in 45:2, read five hundred cubits, as the BSB does.
cultural:
Israel's priests lived under rules about holy food and holy clothing. Portions of certain offerings (grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings) were classed as most holy and had to be eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 6:16, 26; 7:6). Ezekiel's chambers provide that place. The priests' linen garments were also holy. On the Day of Atonement the high priest removed his linen garments in the tent before going out (Leviticus 16:23-24), and Ezekiel extends a similar rule to all priests: they must leave their holy garments in these chambers before going out to the people (verse 14; compare 44:19).

The logic behind these rules is contagion. In priestly thought holiness, like impurity, could be transmitted by contact, and the boundary protected both the holy things and the people. Keeping the holy and the common apart was one of the priests' basic duties (Leviticus 10:10).
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1 to 14 describe the chambers, with dense architectural detail that is hard to follow in places (translations differ on the galleries and passageways of verses 3 to 12), and end with one of the guide's rare speeches explaining their purpose. Verses 15 to 20 are a short, rhythmic summary: the guide measures east, north, south, and west, each side the same, and the final verse gives the reason for the wall. The movement of the whole tour from chapter 40 ends here, back outside the east gate where it began. The closing phrase, "to separate the holy from the common", functions as a caption for chapters 40 to 42.

outline.t: Holy chambers for holy food and holy garments
The outer measurement: a square wall separating the holy from the common

doctrines.note: The wall around the temple exists "to separate the holy from the common" (verse 20). Holiness in the Bible means being set apart for God, and the vision gives it physical shape so that the people will not forget it.

The rules about eating the most holy offerings and changing garments (verses 13 to 14) apply the law of Moses to the restored temple. The vision treats God's ordered worship as something to be carefully kept, not improvised.

The emphasis on separation looks back to the failure that caused the exile: the priests had made no distinction between the holy and the common (22:26). The restored order is designed so that the same defilement cannot happen again.

words.note: Badal, to separate, divide. The same verb is used in Genesis 1 for God separating light from darkness and the waters above from the waters below. Separation is part of how God creates order, and holiness depends on it.
Chol, common, ordinary. Not evil or unclean, but not set apart for God. The Bible's categories are holy and common, clean and unclean; the wall marks the first boundary.
Lishkah, chamber or room. Thirteen times in the chapter. These are rooms attached to the temple for the priests' work, eating, and storage.
Beged, garment. The priests' ministering clothes are holy and must stay in the holy area (verse 14). What touches God's service is set apart from ordinary use.

christ: The New Testament transforms the separation this chapter describes. Paul writes that Christ has broken down the dividing wall of hostility between Jew and Gentile and made both one new people, a holy temple in the Lord (Ephesians 2:14-22). Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and touched lepers and the dead without becoming defiled, because holiness went out from him. Yet the New Testament does not abolish the distinction between holy and common; it relocates it. Believers are called a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5, 9) and told to be holy in all their conduct (1 Peter 1:15-16). In Christ the boundary is not a wall of stone but the line between the life given to God and the life still lived for oneself. The connection is thematic: Ezekiel's wall shows what the gospel both fulfills and moves beyond.
questions: The wall separates the holy from the common, not the good from the bad. What does it mean to set something apart for God that is not in itself wrong?

The priests had to leave their holy garments before going out to the people (verse 14). Why might God care so much about the boundary between worship and ordinary life, and how does the gospel reshape that boundary?
The exile came partly because the priests stopped distinguishing holy from common (22:26). Where do you see that distinction blurred today, in the church or in your own habits?
